strengths: Addresses a clearly important and well-motivated problem: exposure bias / compounding error in autoregressive robot world models, which limits their practical use as simulators.

Non-trivial theoretical contribution: the DiffusionNFT contrastive objective, originally derived for velocity-prediction flow matching models, is carefully re-derived for the x0-prediction (EDM) parameterization used by Ctrl-World, with a full, rigorous proof in the appendix showing the positive/negative branch construction and policy-improvement guarantees transfer exactly.

The proposed 'shared prefix + branched candidates' protocol is a sensible and well-motivated solution to the lack of a fixed prompt in autoregressive video RL, and the randomized prefix-length design is empirically shown to outperform a fixed/curriculum alternative from concurrent work.

Reward design (multi-view, multi-metric, clip-level, group-normalized) is well justified and ablated; the paper shows convincingly that using all three metrics jointly is necessary to avoid degenerate single-metric optimization.

Strong and consistent empirical results: improvements across all reported metrics and cameras versus multiple baselines (WPE, IRASim, Ctrl-World), high paired-comparison win rate (~98%), and a human preference study (80% preference, Elo gap, statistically significant binomial test).
Careful attempt to disentangle 'real' improvements from background bias via object-/robot-centric masked evaluation, which strengthens the claim that gains reflect better interaction modeling.

Extensive, well-organized ablation studies (learning rate, reward composition, prefix sampling strategy, group size/best-of-N, prediction horizon, camera weighting, KL regularization, EMA schedules) that substantiate the design choices.
An additional experiment (Appendix C) evaluating the world model as a policy-ranking/evaluation tool with real-robot correlation adds practical relevance beyond pure visual fidelity metrics.
Clear exposition, good figures, and transparent documentation of implementation details (LoRA setup, optimizer, hardware, sampler) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core RL recipe (DiffusionNFT-style contrastive post-training applied to autoregressive rollout with a prefix-branching scheme) is conceptually very close to concurrent work [36] (WorldCompass); while the paper articulates several differences (random vs. fixed prefix horizon, x0-parameterization derivation, multi-view rewards, masked/human evaluation), the core idea and much of the machinery overlaps, somewhat diminishing the claimed novelty.

The training/RL signal requires access to ground-truth future frames to compute the visual reward, meaning post-training (and presumably any future re-training) depends on paired ground-truth rollouts; the practical implications of this requirement (e.g., applicability to truly open-ended deployment without reference trajectories) are not thoroughly discussed.

Evaluation is performed on a single base architecture/backbone (Ctrl-World, SVD-based, EDM x0-parameterization); no experiments demonstrate the method generalizes to other world-model architectures or velocity-parameterized backbones, despite the appendix claiming parameterization-agnostic guarantees.

The human preference study, while statistically framed, uses only 8 expert raters and self-selected video pairs (raters could choose which pairs to rate), which may introduce selection bias and limits the breadth/diversity of the evaluated preference signal.

The policy-evaluation correlation study in Appendix C is based on very small sample sizes (3 tasks, 3 policies, 5 real and 11 simulated rollouts per task), making the reported Pearson correlation and MMRV improvements only weakly supported statistically.

Evaluated rollout horizons (~11 seconds / 14 clips) are still relatively short for a 'persistent world model' framing; it remains unclear how well the approach scales to substantially longer horizons or more diverse/held-out task distributions.

The method incurs notable computational overhead (K=16 candidates per update, multi-day multi-GPU training), and no direct comparison is provided against other applicable RL/preference-optimization baselines for video diffusion mentioned in related work (e.g., Flow-GRPO, DanceGRPO, DPO-style methods), leaving the relative merit of the specific contrastive-NFT choice versus these alternatives untested.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem for the community — exposure bias / error compounding in autoregressive robot world models — which currently limits the usefulness of these models as simulators.

The theoretical adaptation of the contrastive DiffusionNFT objective from velocity-prediction flow matching to the x0-prediction (EDM) parameterization is carried out rigorously, with a complete, self-contained derivation (Appendix A) showing the policy-improvement guarantee transfers with no extra correction terms.

The group-relative training protocol (shared prefix + K branched candidates + randomized branch depth) is a sensible and non-trivial adaptation of GRPO-style contrastive RL to the closed-loop autoregressive video setting, where no fixed 'prompt' exists.

Strong, consistent empirical results: improvements over the Ctrl-World baseline and other prior world models (WPE, IRASim) across SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS, on both external and wrist cameras, with especially large gains on the task-critical wrist view.

Thorough ablation suite (learning rate, reward composition, prefix curriculum vs. random sampling, group size/best-of-N, prediction horizon, view weighting, KL regularization, EMA schedules) that substantiates the specific design choices made.

Object-/robot-centric masked evaluation and a blind human preference study (with ELO scores and statistical significance testing) corroborate that gains reflect task-relevant dynamics rather than background reconstruction.

The appendix C policy-evaluation correlation study (real vs. simulated task progression) is a nice additional validation of practical utility, showing improved rank correlation and MMRV versus baseline.
weaknesses: The core contribution overlaps substantially with a contemporary work [36] that applies the same contrastive RL post-training paradigm (including a prefix-rollout strategy) to a different conditioned world model; the claimed distinctions (randomized vs. fixed/growing prefix schedule, x0-parameterization derivation, multi-view rewards) are somewhat incremental rather than fundamentally new, which tempers the originality claim.

The human preference study, while statistically significant, uses only 8 expert raters who were allowed to self-select which comparisons to rate, which could introduce selection bias and limits the diversity/generalizability of the preference signal despite the reported inter-rater kappa and p-value.

Absolute quality on the wrist camera remains fairly low (SSIM ~0.67–0.72, LPIPS ~0.28–0.34) and both baseline and proposed method still degrade substantially over the 50-frame horizon (Fig. 5/11), indicating the closed-loop gap is mitigated but far from solved.

The method requires ground-truth future frames as reward targets during post-training (reward is computed against held-out GT), which ties the approach to datasets with available continuation ground truth and may not generalize as easily to settings lacking such paired data (e.g., true open-loop deployment/novel task generalization is not evaluated).

Training cost is high (K=16 candidates per step, 8×H200 GPUs for 3 days), and reproducibility may be a concern for groups without comparable compute; no wall-clock or FLOP comparison against standard fine-tuning is provided beyond the noted overhead.

The policy-evaluation correlation experiment in Appendix C is based on a very small sample (3 tasks × 3 policies × 5 real rollouts), so the reported Pearson correlation/MMRV improvements, while directionally encouraging, are not strongly statistically robust.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: exposure bias/compounding drift in autoregressive robot world models, with clear qualitative and quantitative evidence of the failure mode (Fig. 1, Fig. 3).

Solid technical contribution in adapting the DiffusionNFT contrastive RL objective from velocity-prediction flow matching to the x0-prediction EDM parameterization used by Ctrl-World, with a complete, careful derivation and policy-improvement guarantee (Appendix A) showing the adaptation is not merely heuristic.

Non-trivial engineering solution to the 'no fixed prompt' problem in autoregressive video RL via the shared-prefix/branch-candidate protocol with randomized prefix depth, which is a sensible and well-justified design.

Extensive, multi-faceted empirical validation: SOTA results on DROID across all metrics/views, ~98% pairwise win rate, blind human preference study (80%, with ELO and statistical significance reported), object/robot-centric masked evaluation, generalization to Bridge and RT-1, world-model-based policy evaluation correlation, and a real-robot policy improvement experiment.

Thorough ablation studies (learning rate, reward composition, prefix sampling strategy, group size/best-of-N, prediction horizon, view weighting, KL regularization, EMA schedules) that meaningfully justify the many design choices.
Direct, honest comparisons against a concurrent, closely related work (WorldCompass) and a Self-Forcing-style baseline, clarifying the paper's distinct contributions rather than overstating novelty.
Reasonably clear writing and figures that make a fairly technical RL/diffusion derivation accessible.
weaknesses: The human preference study, while well-designed (2AFC, ELO, significance testing), used only 8 raters; broader rater pools would strengthen the generalizability of the 80% preference claim.

The real-robot policy improvement experiment is limited to a single task family (block picking) with small sample sizes (5 trials/block), which is a fairly narrow test of whether the improved world model actually benefits downstream policy learning.

Baseline comparisons for WPE and IRASim in Table 1 are taken directly from prior papers rather than reproduced under identical evaluation protocol, which could introduce confounds (different validation subsets, camera setups, etc.) not fully controlled for.

The visual fidelity rewards (LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR) are pixel/perceptual proxies without explicit physical or geometric grounding; the paper acknowledges this but the practical impact of this gap (e.g., whether generated rollouts remain physically plausible for downstream policy training beyond the tested picking task) is not deeply probed.

The method is computationally expensive (K=16 candidates, 8×H200 GPUs for 2 days), which may limit reproducibility and broader adoption; this cost is somewhat downplayed relative to its centrality to the approach.

Rollout horizon evaluated (~11s, 14 steps) is useful but still relatively short for claims of 'long-horizon' persistent world models; degradation curves (Fig. 5) show the method still degrades over time, just more slowly, so the practical stable horizon achieved is not fully quantified.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the closed-loop exposure-bias gap in autoregressive robot world models is a genuine and practically important issue for using such models as simulators/evaluators.

Solid theoretical contribution: the paper rigorously re-derives the contrastive DiffusionNFT objective for the x0-prediction (EDM) parameterization, including a full proof (Appendix A) that the optimal predictor moves along a reward-aligned direction; this is more than a superficial adaptation and adds genuine value beyond simply plugging in an existing loss.

Thoughtful protocol design for creating comparable candidate groups in an autoregressive setting (frozen-prefix branching with randomized prefix depth), addressing a real methodological gap between single-image RL post-training and video rollout post-training.

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: SOTA results on DROID across all metrics/views, ~98% paired win-rate, 80% human preference rate with a well-documented and reasonably rigorous human study (expert raters, ELO, statistical significance, bias controls such as randomized position and masked reference).

Goes beyond raw visual metrics with object-/robot-centric masked evaluation, policy-evaluation correlation with real robot rollouts, an actual policy-improvement experiment on real hardware, and generalization results on Bridge and RT-1 — this breadth substantially strengthens the practical significance claims.

Very thorough ablation suite (13 tables) isolating essentially every design choice (LR, reward composition, prefix sampling, group size/best-of-N, prediction horizon, view weighting, KL regularization, EMA schedules), which supports reproducibility and gives confidence the reported configuration is well justified rather than cherry-picked.

Honest and specific comparison against a concurrent, closely related work (WorldCompass), including a controlled reward-substitution experiment (HPSv3 vs. their reward) that isolates the source of improvement rather than just asserting novelty.
weaknesses: Computational cost is high (K=16 candidates per update, autoregressive rollout generation dominating cost, 2 days on 8×H200), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze in terms of scalability trade-offs versus alternative cheaper approaches (e.g., best-of-2 ablation suggests smaller K may suffice, but this isn't the deployed configuration).

The real-robot policy-improvement experiment is fairly limited in scope (single task family, 4-block spatial picking, only 5 trials per block condition), which is a small sample for drawing strong conclusions about downstream policy-improvement utility, even though it is a nice addition.

The reward is purely perceptual (LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR); as the authors note, it does not explicitly enforce physical/geometric consistency, so gains in pixel-level fidelity may not fully translate to physically plausible dynamics — this is appropriately flagged as future work but remains a real limitation of the current instantiation.

Concurrent overlap with WorldCompass on the core contrastive-RL-for-autoregressive-world-models paradigm slightly reduces the perceived novelty of contribution #1, even though the paper clarifies real differences (x0 vs. v-pred, randomized vs. fixed prefix horizon, reward design, additional validation).

Some quantitative gains, while consistent and statistically validated, are numerically modest in places (e.g., external SSIM 0.84→0.86), so the practical significance of the improvement for downstream tasks like policy evaluation rests more on the qualitative/human-study/policy-correlation evidence than on the core pixel metrics alone.

The human preference study, while well-designed, uses only 8 expert raters; broader rater diversity (e.g., non-expert users, larger N) would strengthen generalizability of the preference claims, though the statistical significance reported partially mitigates this concern.
